note: The answer correctly blames the method and cites the atmospheric-exposure reason and the DO/Eh/temperature restriction but omits the qualified-reporting allowance the in-situ-vs-recommended distinction the anoxic/reducing inert-gas restriction and the suction-lift pump warning. Unmet: Explains bailed/decanted samples cannot establish unqualified ambient Eh; acknowledges the subsample section permits estimated explicitly qualified reporting; States ORP DO and temperature are required to be measured in situ where possible while pH conductivity and turbidity are only recommended to be; States that in anoxic or reducing groundwater subsample procedures must not be used at all unless handled under an inert gas; Warns that a peristaltic or other suction-lift pump also must not be used for ORP or DO because negative pressure volatilises dissolved gases

The answer correctly states the low-pH compensation error and its ~50 percent magnitude but omits the hydrogen-ion share-of-conductance cause the largest-source-of-error note the 25 °C equilibration check with its ±5 μS/cm / ±3 percent bar and the comment-field recording requirement. Unmet: explains the cause as the hydrogen ion having different transport properties from other ions and contributing a large share of the conductance at low pH; states that at low pH the temperature correction can be the single largest source of error in the measurement; describes the check of comparing the in-situ reading against the same water equilibrated to 25 C; gives the pass bar for that check as within about 5 microsiemens per centimetre at or below 100 or about 3 percent above that; states that if an alternative low-pH compensation method is used the compensation factor has to be recorded in the comment field

The answer gives the 15-20 min/10 min/30 min recording schedule and lists temperature and pH to log but omits the airtight/oxygen-impermeable setup the >30 min drift the slow asymmetric ORP response the nearest-10 mV reporting and the electrode system while inventing no forbidden tolerance or over-precise Eh. Unmet: Measurement made in situ or through an airtight flow-through system that eliminates aeration; Tubing impermeable to oxygen fittings airtight atmospheric oxygen purged before measuring; Reading drifts until thermal equilibrium which can take longer than 30 minutes; ORP responds more slowly than pH and asymmetrically longer in one direction; Calculated Eh reported to the nearest 10 mV; Temperature electrode system used and pH at time of measurement recorded with the value

The answer makes only the temperature-change-during-transport point and never addresses the turbidity bench-measurement biases (condensation cell orientation coloured water gas bubbles dirty cells) or the need to check both methods though it avoids the prohibited assertions. Unmet: Identifies condensation on the sample cell as a plausible source of bias when sample water is much colder than air without establishing it as the actual cause.; Names the other bench-measurement biases in the same family: cell orientation coloured water gas bubbles and scratched or dirty sample cells.; Explains the preference for in-situ or pumped dynamic measurement while requiring checks of both methods before deciding which reading is reliable.; Notes that letting the sample equilibrate to ambient temperature reduces condensation but warming the sample can change particle associations in the water.

The answer makes none of the must-contain points: it never says the 4/7/10 set is insufficient never gives the 1.68–10 working range bracketing requirement the ±10 °C buffer-temperature condition or the ±0.05 pH unit check and instead asserts the standard buffers are adequate for the acidic sample. Unmet: States the usual 4/7/10 buffer set is not sufficient for acidic water and a pH 1.68 (or 2) buffer is needed when acidic waters are measured; States the standard pH procedure is expected to be accurate over roughly pH 1.68 to 10; States the sample pH must fall inside the calibrated range so a 4/7/10 set does not bracket pH 3.2; States the calibration buffers must be within about 10 C of the sample temperature; States that a check of the buffer nearest the sample pH should be within about 0.05 pH unit of its value at that temperature or the system is recalibrated

The answer states the subsample qualifier requirement for turbidity temperature DO and Eh but never says a discrete turbidity sample must not be taken from the flow-cell discharge gives no storage limits and does not note turbidity's time sensitivity or on-site/in-situ preference. Unmet: States plainly that a discrete turbidity sample must not be collected from the discharge passing through the flow-through chamber holding the other sensors; Gives the storage limits if the sample cannot be read on site: clean amber bottle kept out of sunlight chilled at or below 4 C held no longer than 24 hours; Notes turbidity is time sensitive and should be measured on site preferably in situ

The answer gives the per-degree range the linear formula the 0.019–0.020 factor and the 25 °C reference but omits the ±5 percent accuracy statement for 5–35 °C and pH 4–11 so not every must-contain point is made. Unmet: States temperature compensation is typically accurate to ±5 percent for 5-35 °C and pH 4-11

The answer correctly gives the barometric-pressure and temperature recording requirements but omits the one-point calibration goal the computed-concentration/ionic-strength basis the recalibrate-if-droplets step and the salinity-correction timing and recalibration consequences. Unmet: Goal of one-point calibration: 100% oxygen-saturated environment with DO sensor and temperature sensor at same temperature; Reported concentration computed from sensor signal with temperature and ionic strength; sensor does not measure mg/L directly; Ionic strength for salinity correction estimated from the conductivity measurement; Checks for droplets on optical module and temperature sensor recalibrates if present; does not assume an unidentified probe is optical; USGS prefers applying manual salinity correction after calibration and measurement; distinguishes automatic conductivity-based compensation; Manual salinity correction at calibration forces recalibration for each change in field salinity

The answer gives the ±0.2 °C accuracy requirement and a verification against a certified/traceable sensor but omits the 'verification not adjustment' distinction and the faulty-thermistor effect on specific conductance. Unmet: Checking means verifying accuracy across the range of use not adjusting to a standard like pH/conductivity; A faulty or drifting thermistor in the conductivity cell produces wrong specific conductance values

The answer gives no per-parameter stabilization tolerances (temperature SC DO pH turbidity) and no 60-second thermal-equilibrium minimum and it violates a must-not by applying a single 10% tolerance to turbidity and other in-situ parameters. Unmet: temperature criterion about ±0.2 °C; specific conductance criterion ±5 µS/cm at or below 100 ±3% above; dissolved oxygen criterion about ±0.2 mg/L; pH criterion about ±0.1 unit; turbidity stabilization ±0.5 TU or ±5% whichever greater at or below 100 TU; ±10% above 100 TU; minimum wait in surface water at least 60 seconds for thermal equilibrium; 60 seconds is a minimum and some instruments need longer per manufacturer

The answer makes only the ZoBell-check point omitting the temperature-dependent table value the ~430 mV at 25 C interpolation thermal-equilibration timing the 5 mV calculated-Eh pass window and the 90-day chilled stability though it violates no 'must not' item. Unmet: States expected ZoBell value is temperature dependent and must be read from the temperature table not taken as a single number; Gives theoretical ZoBell Eh at 25 C as about 430 mV; States values for temperatures between table rows are interpolated; States solution and sensors must reach thermal equilibrium on the order of 15 to 30 minutes before the check is read; Gives check pass window as calculated Eh after adding reference-electrode potential to measured potential within 5 mV of the temperature-specific table value; States ZoBell's solution is reported stable for at least 90 days chilled at 4 C; does not invent a 90-day expiry

The answer correctly states the two tables agree and are not stricter but omits that the general chapter points multiparameter users to the multiparameter chapter omits the sensor-accuracy-varies-by-model point and omits the persistent-variability procedure. Unmet: States the general field-measurement chapter itself points multiparameter users to the multiparameter chapter for criteria of the same kind; States the criteria are standard sensor stabilisation criteria and that actual sensor accuracy varies by model and manufacturer which is a separate matter; For persistent variability extends equilibration and records additional measurements then either reports the median of the final five or more readings or selects a representative final reading using site knowledge and professional judgment documenting the decision

The answer makes the low-ionic-strength cause the circuit-completion explanation the KCl fix at ~150 µS/cm and the try-normal-first sequencing but omits the sample/buffer ionic-strength and liquid-junction causes the alternative electrode recommendation the <0.01 pH figure and the warning against stirring; no must-not item is violated. Unmet: Names large ionic-strength difference between sample and buffers and enlarged liquid-junction potential as contributing causes; Recommends a different electrode type (fast-responding liquid-filled Ross combination or double-junction); States the KCl addition changes the measured pH by less than about 0.01 unit; Warns against stirring the untreated low-conductance subsample to speed stabilization while permitting gentle swirling to dissolve KCl

The answer states the 0.3 mg/L variation exceeds the ±0.2 mg/L criterion but it frames the criterion as a saturation performance check rather than a five-or-more-consecutive-reading stability rule and it omits the median/representative-reading rule and the ORP exception. Unmet: Gives the USGS stabilisation criterion for optical DO as about ±0.2 mg/L across five or more consecutive readings; Allows longer equilibration and additional readings then either the median of the final five or more readings or a representative final reading selected using site knowledge and professional judgment with the decision documented; Gives the median rule as the final three or more readings in surface water or the final five or more in groundwater; Notes that ORP is not covered by that stabilisation table and is instead judged by the potential holding constant over the reading sequence

The answer correctly places the pH sensor downstream of conductivity but omits the close-to-source/shielded-from-sunlight point and the flow-cell-design-dependent probe position point. Unmet: states the flow cell should be kept as close to the source water as possible and shielded from direct sunlight; notes the specific-conductance probe position relative to the pH electrode depends on the flow-cell design

The answer is a bare refusal stating it lacks information on calibration order so it makes none of the required points even though the rubric expected a real answer. Unmet: states order matters and temperature first; gives specific conductance next before pH; gives remaining order pH DO ORP turbidity ion-selective/fluorescence with A6.2 DO-last exception; rationale: low to high ionic strength so residual standard cannot bias next calibration; conductivity before pH because pH buffers/filling solutions are high ionic strength contamination source; sensors rinsed three times with deionized water between standards; sonde calibrated or checked before each field use

The answer correctly states A6.4's 0.05 pH-unit final-buffer check but declines the A6.8 example-form criteria (±0.1 pH unit; ±0.3 below 75 µS/cm) and so never draws the required distinction while avoiding all the 'must not' violations. Unmet: Attributes ±0.1 pH unit to the A6.8 example field form's calibration criterion; Attributes ±0.3 pH unit below 75 µS/cm to that example form; Distinguishes the form's conductivity-dependent criteria from A6.4's final-buffer check requiring agreement within 0.05 pH unit of the certified value at calibration temperature

The answer makes the daily-calibration and midday-drift points but omits the sampling-location exemption the deployment/recovery check the DO post-calibration check details and the QA-plan drift-criteria condition and it violates a must-not by asserting the EPA SOP 'sets a different calibration schedule than the USGS guidance' without any support for the USGS side. Unmet: EPA spot-sampling cadence includes an end-of-day calibration check except when the instrument is calibrated at each sampling location under the stated exemption; A continuously deployed sonde is calibrated before deployment and its calibration checked on recovery; The DO post-calibration check is done in measurement mode recording DO temperature and barometric pressure for comparison against an oxygen-solubility chart; The SOP's own drift criteria apply only when the project quality assurance plan does not specify its own

The answer correctly covers DO and pH temperature dependence but omits specific conductance and ORP as affected channels and never notes the temperature sensor's separate location from the pH electrode. Unmet: Identifies pH DO specific conductance and ORP as potentially affected; does not assume pod wiring/compensation configuration; Explains specific conductance is a temperature-corrected value computed from measured temperature; Notes the temperature sensor typically sits in a different part of the instrument from the pH electrode

The answer names only the EPA chart and omits every required figure and comparison — no 9.09 or 9.06 mg/L values no 0.03 mg/L difference no Benson and Krause note and no ±0.2 mg/L tolerance comparison — so no must-contain point is made. Unmet: gives the USGS table value at 20.0 C and 760 mmHg as about 9.09 mg/L; gives the EPA chart value at 20 C and 760 mmHg as about 9.06 mg/L; states the difference is 0.03 mg/L and assesses its significance against the applicable procedure; notes the USGS values are generated from the Benson and Krause equations; compares the 0.03 mg/L difference with the USGS saturation-check tolerance of ±0.2 mg/L; advises using the table belonging to whichever protocol the work is being done under consistently rather than mixing them

The answer misses every must-contain point and violates a must-not item by telling the operator the raw conductivity reading can be used directly in the salinity correction lookup with no fixing required. Unmet: states the salinity correction table is indexed on specific conductance referenced to 25 C not raw conductivity at the water's own temperature; states a conductivity reading taken at any other temperature must be corrected to what it would read at 25 C before use; states most modern meters and sondes apply that temperature compensation automatically and report the 25 C value; tells the operator to confirm whether the pod's conductivity output is already temperature-compensated; notes A6.2 defines saline waters as specific conductance greater than 2 000 microsiemens per centimetre where the correction varies with instrument type calibration method and salts in solution

The answer gives the annual cadence and a certified/traceable reference check but misses the distinction that a temperature sensor is verified rather than adjusted to a standard the ±0.2 °C accuracy requirement for a multiparameter sensor correcting another parameter and the probe/temperature-sensor coverage and moisture-evaporation point. Unmet: States a temperature sensor is not adjusted to a standard like a pH/conductivity sensor; the procedure verifies accuracy across the range of use; Gives required accuracy as about ±0.2 °C where the sensor is bundled on a multiparameter instrument and used to correct another parameter; States calibration solution must cover probe and temperature sensor; identifies evaporation of moisture as a DO air-calibration concern

The answer withholds the requested factor (0.8235) saying it is not in the excerpts which is a refusal of the figure the rubric asks for even though it correctly states the multiplication step and cites table 6.2-4. Unmet: Gives 0.8235 as the factor for 20.0 °C at 50 000 µS/cm

The answer states the 2 000 µS/cm threshold from the manual but never asks for the upstream specific conductance and instead assumes freshwater means an essentially 1.0 factor so it misses both must-contain points; no must-not item is violated. Unmet: Explains the manual's operational saline-water correction applies above 2 000 µS/cm and asks for the upstream specific conductance before deciding; freshwater does not imply zero conductivity or mathematically zero salinity effect; Gives 1.0000 at zero specific conductance without extending that exact factor to all freshwater

The answer misses the EPA chart's 45 °C and 690 mmHg bounds the salinity-correction point and the simultaneous-limit explanation and it extrapolates temperature coverage past the tabulated 40 °C limit by declaring the needed range covered. Unmet: EPA chart's temperature coverage runs to 45 C and gives no value above that; EPA chart bottoms out around 690 mmHg; Explains the different table bounds and that neither printed table covers simultaneous temperature above 40 °C and pressure below 690 mmHg; supported generated values require a separate source; Notes only the USGS chapter supplies salinity correction factors which the EPA chart does not carry
All five must-contain points are stated correctly with supporting quotes and no must-not item (invented percentage always-representative claim or invented increment count) appears.

The answer vaguely discourages diluting a high-turbidity standard but never states the rule for commercial calibration solutions omits the 4 000-unit formazin exception the suspension-matrix/nonlinearity explanation and the recommendation to buy prepared solutions; no must-not item is violated. The answer correctly gives the median of the final stabilized readings as the logged value but never mentions the ~60-second equilibration window or that the per-vertical value is the median of readings taken within about 60 seconds of equilibration. Unmet: States sensors need at least 60 seconds to equilibrate or the manufacturer's stated time; States the value recorded at each vertical is the median of the values observed within about 60 seconds after the sensors have equilibrated

The answer acknowledges pressure dependence and that salinity lowers saturation but it uses 695 mmHg table values (9.11 and 8.30 mg/L a 0.8 drop) instead of the ~10.0/9.0 mg/L at 760 mmHg and the 0.99 mg/L benchmark and it never says the warming contribution itself cannot be established from these readings alone. Unmet: Gives freshwater oxygen solubility at ~15 C from the USGS table (roughly 10.0-10.1 mg/L near 760 mmHg); Gives freshwater oxygen solubility at ~20 C from the same table (roughly 9.0-9.1 mg/L near 760 mmHg); States freshwater equilibrium solubility at 760 mmHg falls by 0.99 mg/L from 15 C to 20 C as a conditional benchmark not a ceiling; States the actual warming contribution and remaining site-specific drop cannot be established from these readings alone (pressure salinity initial saturation not given)

The answer rejects the old calibrant on shelf-life grounds but never mentions flocculation or the need to distinguish reversible settling from flocculation so the flocculated-suspension point is missed and the check-and-reject point is only partially made. Unmet: States that calibrants with flocculated suspensions must not be used; Requires checking whether the settled layer is reversible settling or flocculation along with labeled expiry and storage compliance; rejects flocculated expired or compromised calibrant rather than assuming all settled calibrant must be discarded

The answer refuses and withholds the requested value which the provided table does contain so it makes none of the must-contain points. Unmet: Gives 9.09 mg/L for 20.0 °C at 760 mmHg; Attributes the value to the freshwater table in the USGS NFM chapter on dissolved oxygen (table 6.2-2); States the figure is for fresh water before any salinity correction

The answer gives a ±0.2 mg/L zero-check tolerance and generic recalibration/troubleshooting advice but never states the 0.5 mg/L zero-solution value the cleaning/membrane/electrolyte remedy or the accuracy-dependence of that value so no must-contain point is made. Unmet: States the instrument should read less than 0.5 mg/L in a 0.0 mg/L DO solution; States a reading above 0.5 mg/L or any negative reading calls for cleaning the probe and changing the membrane and electrolyte; Notes the 0.5 mg/L value assumes an instrument accuracy of about ±0.2 mg/L and may be adjusted to the project's or instrument's accuracy requirements

Only the ±0.2 mg/L agreement/verification point is made; the answer omits the wet sponge/towel setup the no-touch rule the 10–15 minute saturation time (giving 5–10 instead) and the on-site barometer requirement though it avoids the prohibited inventions and does not put the probe in water. Unmet: 100 percent water-saturated air environment made with a wet sponge or wet paper towel in the bottom of the container; Neither the probe nor the temperature sensor may touch the wet sponge or towel; Roughly 10 to 15 minutes for the confined air to saturate while the instrument warms up; Barometric pressure must come from an on-site barometer not a weather service unless corrected for elevation
All three must-contain points are made correctly (6.95 mg/L at 35 °C/760 mmHg a ~2.14 mg/L decrease both values from the same USGS table) and no must-not item appears.

The answer gives the <3 µS/cm DIW criterion and treats 6 µS/cm as a failure but never explains that this is the meter's low-end zero-response check made with the dry cell in air or in deionized water. Unmet: Explains this is the meter's low-end zero-response check made with the dry cell in air or in deionized water

The answer correctly bars deionized water as a calibration standard and distinguishes it from the permitted zero-response check and gives a nearest/bracketing standard with a 500 µS/cm example but it omits the reason that sub-200 µS/cm standards are easily biased by dilution/contamination and never says the standard must be certified and instrument-compatible; no must-not item is violated and the USGS source is not cited. Unmet: States calibration standards greater than 200 µS/cm are recommended because lower ones are easily biased by dilution or contamination; States the standard should be nearest to or bracketing the expected sample value and selects a certified instrument-compatible standard on that basis; 500 µS/cm is one supported example

The answer gives the temperature DO pH and consecutive-reading criteria correctly but omits the specific-conductance tolerance entirely and gives only the ≤100 TU turbidity criterion missing the 'whichever is greater' clause and the >100 TU ±10 percent rule. Unmet: Specific conductance ±5 µS/cm at ≤100 µS/cm and ±3 percent above 100 µS/cm; Turbidity ±0.5 TU or ±5 percent whichever greater at ≤100 TU; ±10 percent above 100 TU

The answer makes the two-point minimum the ±2 °C extrema rule the ±4 °C mean rule and the 6/10 °C example but never states the at-most-five-points limit; no must-not item is violated. Unmet: Notes the procedure requires at most five points without generalizing
All three must-contain points are made (0.40 at nearest 0.05 64 at nearest 1 both cited to the USGS reporting-convention table excerpt) and no must-not item is violated.

The answer covers both acceptable methods and the in situ annual route but never states the required one-point check immediately before a field trip. Unmet: States a one-point check against a certified sensor is also required immediately before a field trip

The answer correctly says EPA 180.1 rounding differs from USGS/ASTM and cites the 43.12→45 example but it never gives the EPA-rounded values for 0.42 (0.40) or 63.7 (65) and never states the USGS-follows-ASTM-unless-drinking-water-compliance note naming EPA 180.1 GLI Method 2 or ISO 7027. Unmet: States EPA Method 180.1 also reports 0.42 as 0.40 to the nearest 0.05 unit below 1.; States EPA Method 180.1 reports 63.7 as 65 to the nearest 5 units in the 40 to under 100 range.; Notes USGS follows ASTM guidelines unless the data were collected for drinking-water compliance under EPA 180.1 GLI Method 2 or ISO 7027.

The answer gives the 60-second minimum the thermal-equilibrium rationale and the manufacturer-guidelines caveat but never notes that equilibration can run from 60 seconds to several minutes depending on the temperature difference. Unmet: Notes equilibration can run from 60 seconds to several minutes depending on the temperature difference

The answer asserts the probe's raw ORP millivolts are the Eh value the USGS chapters refer to making them interchangeable and never reaching the standard hydrogen electrode reference which violates the 'must not' items and misses every 'must contain' point. Unmet: states that Eh is defined relative to the standard hydrogen electrode; states that Eh is an equilibrium potential developed at the boundary between a noble-metal electrode and the water reflecting redox-active species in solution; states that the probe's millivolts are not Eh on their own because the raw reading is against the probe's own reference electrode; states that getting Eh means adding the reference electrode's own potential to the measured reading
All three must-contain points are stated (15–30 min equilibration ~30 min stabilization and recording drift with no single value possible) and no must-not item is violated.

The answer correctly grounds the check in ZoBell's solution before field use but omits the temperature-corrected table comparison the 430 mV theoretical value at 25 °C and the stabilization-before-recording requirement while committing no must-not violations. Unmet: States the calculated Eh of ZoBell's must come within 5 mV of the table value for the solution's temperature; Gives 430 mV as the theoretical Eh of ZoBell's at 25 °C; States the reading must stabilize to within ±5 mV before the temperature and millivolt value are recorded

The answer correctly notes ORP's absence from the stabilization-criteria table and names the five listed parameters but never states that Eh is not treated as a routine or direct field measurement. Unmet: States Eh is not treated as a routine or direct field measurement

The answer correctly states that a required-procedure departure must be documented and independently quality assured but never says the same expectation applies to departures from recommended procedures. Unmet: notes the same documentation-plus-independent-QA expectation applies to departures from recommended procedures

All three must-contain points are stated (required = established policy to be followed as written; recommended = several acceptable alternatives; reasons for the selection must be documented) and no must-not item is triggered since the answer still requires justification/record for recommended choices; note the citations point to the pH chapter rather than the two should-cite documents.

The answer correctly states the label is dictated by instrument design rather than preference but omits the wavelength-to-unit correspondence the detector-geometry rule and the expansion of NTU/FNU. Unmet: Broad-spectrum 400-680 nm light corresponds to NTU NTRU BU AU NTMU; FNU FNRU FBU FAU FNMU correspond to 780-900 nm near-infrared; Detector arrangement sets the other half: 90 degrees = nephelometry plain labels; backscatter attenuation ratio multibeam each have distinct labels; Expands the letters for at least NTU (nephelometric turbidity units) and FNU (formazin nephelometric units)

The answer correctly defines TU as a generic turbidity-units label and notes the method is unspecified but it never says the label fails to reveal the light source/optical arrangement and never mentions the historical JTU/FTU labels. Unmet: states that because the instrument design is unknown the label does not tell you what light source or optical arrangement produced the number; warns that older data can also carry historical labels - Jackson turbidity units (JTU) or formazin turbidity units (FTU) - which are no longer in normal use

The answer correctly states no conversion is needed because mho/cm and S/cm are the same unit but omits the 1971 changeover the interchangeable terminology and the temperature-reference caveat. Unmet: Mhos were the normal reporting unit for older data with the changeover around 1971; Specific conductance specific electrical conductance and electrical conductivity are all used in the literature for this same measurement; Because electrical conductivity is not always referenced to a standard temperature the measurement or reference temperature has to be reported and checked against older values

The answer correctly states the isolation and bubble-free-surface difficulties of sensor-only immersion but omits the practical rinsing/agitation steps and the steady-stand step and violates no must-not item. Unmet: Notes practical steps: rinse with deionized water then the standard and work bubbles off by agitating the sonde or running the wiper before reading; Notes the sonde is set steady — stood vertically on a flat surface or held in a stand — rather than hand-held

The answer gives the 5-percent hydrochloric acid soak and the manufacturer-guidance check but omits the detergent-first step and the warning against nitric acid/aqua regia; no must-not item is violated. Unmet: says to start with a detergent solution and only escalate to acid if that fails; warns that nitric acid aqua regia and anything else that etches platinum or gold must not be used because they will attack platinum and platinum-iridium electrodes

The answer correctly presents both immersion methods as manufacturer-dependent but omits the separate-vessel/not-in-water-body condition and gives only the volume side of the trade-off not the contamination/dilution risk. Unmet: States either way the calibration is done in a separate vessel with the sensor sitting in the calibration standard not in the water body being monitored; Gives the trade-off for putting the whole head in: it takes a lot more standard and brings a risk of contaminating or diluting that standard

The answer correctly defines specific conductance as the conductance of 1 cm³ of solution at 25 °C and says the unit is a property of the water but it omits the resistance/siemens basis the cell-constant (spacing/area) relation and the distinction that µS/cm alone does not establish temperature compensation. Unmet: Explains conductance is the inverse of the water's electrical resistance measured in siemens; Explains conductivity = conductance × cell constant (electrode spacing / electrode area) a geometry-normalized property; Distinguishes conductivity from specific conductance at 25 °C; µS/cm alone does not establish temperature compensation so the reference temperature must be checked
The answer gives the 2-hour maximum soak the thorough deionized-water rinse afterwards and defers to the manufacturer's guidance with no prohibited soak time or wrong-probe content.

The answer warns the swap is not plug-and-play and that replacing cables may require recertification and it invents no interval cost or provider and does not confuse recertification with routine calibration of other sensors.
All four must-contain points are stated (24-hour limit ≤4°C chilling clean amber bottle out of sunlight and holding framed as a fallback) and no must-not item is violated.

The answer names connections and weak batteries but omits the cable break and does not distinguish erratic-reading causes from dirty-sensor/expired-verification causes of inaccurate readings (it even attributes dirty-sensor buildup to erratic readings). Unmet: Points at a break somewhere in the cable; Distinguishes the erratic-reading checks from dirty-sensor and expired-verification causes of inaccurate readings noting weak batteries can cause either

The answer correctly declines to adopt 1.0 mg/L and says the configured threshold is unavailable but it omits the spectrophotometric verification trigger and the Rhodazine D 0.025–1.0 mg/L range. Unmet: States that anticipated DO below 1.0 mg/L triggers instrument-specific spectrophotometric verification for optical sensors before reporting not an alarm at or below 1.0 mg/L; Notes that the Rhodazine D spectrophotometric method covers roughly 0.025 to 1.0 mg/L underscoring that the figure is about verifying the instrument not judging the water

The answer correctly declines and says the pod threshold is unavailable but it never gives the USGS 6.5–8.5 river-water description nor frames it as a general description rather than a limit citing measurement ranges instead. Unmet: States USGS pH chapter describes river waters not affected by contamination as generally reading pH 6.5 to 8.5 attributed to that chapter; Makes clear this is a description of what such waters generally read not a criterion or limit the chapter sets

The answer correctly says not to shake and to invert about 25 times but omits the one-second inversion cycle the instruction to let bubbles clear before filling the cell and the guidance about avoiding reading straight from the bottle (pouring off immediately if unavoidable). Unmet: says to mix by turning the bottle end over end about 25 times roughly one turn per second; says to let the bubbles clear before filling the measurement cell; notes that reading straight from the bottle into the cell is best avoided and that if it cannot be avoided the sample is poured off immediately after mixing so the particles do not settle out

The answer presents the 1.0 mg/L figure as a definition of hypoxic-to-anoxic conditions (an ecological limit) and applies it to the pod's reading missing the verification-discussion attribution and the unavailable-threshold statements and violating the must-not against presenting the figure as an ecological limit. Unmet: Attributes the below-1.0 mg/L hypoxic-to-anoxic wording to the USGS optical-sensor verification discussion not a universal ecological definition; States that the 1.0 mg/L figure is the point at which the chapter requires an optical sensor's accuracy in that range to be independently documented before such data are reported not an ecological limit it sets for the pod; States that this pod's configured threshold is unavailable here; no supplied result establishes whether one is configured

The answer declines to set an alarm band and says the pod's configured threshold is unavailable but it never states the chapter's 6.5–8.5 river-water description the 6.0–8.5 groundwater figure or the distinction between a described range and a configured limit. Unmet: States 6.5–8.5 is the chapter's description of uncontaminated river water not a recommended configuration limit; States most U.S. groundwaters run 6.0 to 8.5 so one freshwater figure doesn't fit both surface and groundwater; Distinguishes the range the chapter describes from a limit configured for the pod

The answer correctly declines to adopt 19 NTU and says the pod threshold is unavailable but it omits the chapter's observed groundwater turbidity figures the observation-not-recommendation point and the qualitative nature of turbidity. Unmet: Chapter reports natural groundwater turbidity up to 19 units and contaminated groundwater can run higher attributed to chapter; Chapter's groundwater figures describe observations not a recommended flagging value; Turbidity is a relative qualitative indicator not a numeric pass/fail band

The answer correctly states not to insert the electrode in the stock bottle to pour into a separate container and to discard the used solution but omits the recommendation to decant into a labelled dedicated secondary bottle for field use. Unmet: Recommends decanting into a dedicated secondary bottle for field use labelled with value lot number and expiration date

The answer is a bare refusal that makes none of the required must-contain points withholding the supported storage expiration temperature and logbook guidance the rubric expected. Unmet: States that the decanted field bottles should be refreshed before every field trip; States that solution past its expiration date must not be used; States that the solutions must be protected from wide temperature swings and from extreme heat or freezing; States that solution which has been frozen or overheated can no longer be assumed valid and should be discarded; Notes that the lot number expiration date and the temperature at use are recorded in the instrument logbook
